messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi had spent much of the first years of his marriage trying not to think in images. What he could not avoid were the moments that caught him unprepared: the stale, sweet smell of alcohol drifting out of a restaurant doorway, a burst of incomprehensible chatter in a crowded corridor, or the flat, sick feeling that came over him when he had a fever or an unsettled stomach. In each of those moments his body seemed to move before his mind could catch up. His chest tightened, his shoulders rose, and he found himself scanning for the nearest exit, already jumpy, already certain that something was wrong. As an architect, he worked in open-plan offices and spent time moving between noisy sites and meetings; when a subcontractor spoke over another in rapid, overlapping language, Ravi would go rigid and lose track of the conversation, then leave the room telling himself he needed air. He had come to believe that his own reactions were proof that he could not trust himself to do the right thing when it mattered, and that belief sat alongside a deeper shame: he had failed in his most important role in life by not keeping himself safe, and by failing to see what his partner was capable of until it was too late.

The trauma itself came back to him in fragments, each one sharp as a photograph. His former romantic partner had been drinking heavily that evening, and Ravi remembered the alcohol on his breath before he remembered the words. There had been a sudden barrage of angry speech, some of it blurred and impossible to follow, then the first blow and the sick, terror-filled awareness that he was trapped in a room with someone he had trusted. When he tried later to describe it, he could only manage a few moments at a time, each scene held in his mind as if he were looking at separate pictures: the raised hand, the overturned chair, the look on the other man’s face. Remembering it brought back the same terror he had felt then, so vividly that his body would respond before he had fully formed the thought. A smell in a bar, a snatch of loud, indistinct conversation, or waking with a headache and fever would suddenly press the event back into the room with him. His pulse would race, his muscles would tense, and the memory would sharpen into those isolated still frames, making the abuse feel present rather than past. In those moments he became even more convinced that he had been naive, that he had betrayed his own judgment, and that his inability to see danger sooner meant he could not trust himself now.

Over time Ravi began to organise his days around staying ahead of that bodily alarm. He went to bed later and later because he needed to stay alert, listening for sounds in the house and checking the locks more than once, and lying awake only made him more jumpy the next day. When his body felt unwell—whether from a cold, a migraine, or simple exhaustion—he interpreted the sensation as the start of danger, and the unease spread quickly into the old terror. At work he avoided the lunch places where alcohol was served and declined client dinners whenever he could, quietly shrinking his social world. Even in his own office, a burst of incomprehensible chatter from the conference room could pull him back into the memory of being shouted at, and he would leave the door half-open, watch the hallway, and struggle to return to the plan on his screen. The more vigilant he became, the more readily his body reacted, and each reaction seemed to confirm that something terrible was near. That constant alertness made the memories more intrusive and more vivid; in turn, every flash of the event deepened his sense that he had failed and could not rely on his own judgment. He spoke of himself with a kind of grim certainty, saying that a man who had let betrayal happen once could not be counted on to protect his marriage or handle pressure at work.

By the time he came to therapy, Ravi was exhausted by the smallness of the life he had built around these alarms. His wife had noticed that he was withdrawn at home, hesitant to go out, and often preoccupied with scanning rooms and monitoring his own body. What brought him in was a recent episode after a flu-like illness, when feeling physically unwell triggered the old terror so strongly that he sat on the bathroom floor for nearly an hour, shaking and unable to settle. He said he was most afraid that this would never stop—that his body would keep warning him of danger before he could think, and that he would continue to live as though the betrayal were happening again. At the same time, he admitted a quieter hope: that if he could understand why alcohol smell, confused voices, and feeling ill were pulling him back into those stolen moments, he might begin to trust his own mind again and reclaim the parts of his marriage and work that fear had narrowed.
